sources.quote: Dear Sphinx, Your aphorisms must appear in the second number of the Chameleon: they are exquisite. 'The Priest and the Acolyte' is not by Dorian: though you were right in discerning by internal evidence that the author has a profile. He is an undergraduate of strange beauty. The story is, to my ears, too direct: there is no nuance: it profanes a little by revelation: God and other artists are always a little obscure. Still, it has interesting qualities, and is at moments poisonous: which is something. Ever yours
sources.context: Wilde to Ada Leverson, [early December 1894], Albemarle Club (MS Clark) - quoted whole. The editors identify the anonymous author as John Francis Bloxam, editor of The Chameleon and an undergraduate of Exeter College, and record that the story was attributed to Wilde and that 'much play was made' with it at his trial - along with Wilde's own aphorisms in the same issue and Douglas's poem 'Two Loves'. 'Dorian' here is John Gray, who is on this map.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde's only recorded description of him - and his verdict on the story that would be used against him.
sources.provenance: PDF page 677; printed folio 625 confirmed on the rendered page image.

name: John Francis Bloxam
bio: An undergraduate of Exeter College, Oxford, who founded and edited The Chameleon and wrote for its first and only issue, anonymously, 'The Priest and the Acolyte' - a story of a priest's love for a boy. The story was widely attributed to Wilde, and much was made of it at his trial. Wilde, who had aphorisms in the same issue, described its author privately as 'an undergraduate of strange beauty'.
bio_note: No letters between them survive: he has no entry in the Index of Recipients, and the evidence here is a sentence in a letter to [[leverson]] (printed 625, read at the page). Dates not recorded and none inferred.
